category.label: Betaine
category.comparisonNote: Betaine anhydrous (trimethylglycine / TMG) and betaine hydrochloride (HCl) are distinct forms with different research and marketed uses. HCl compound mass is not converted to anhydrous betaine or treated as a sports-performance equivalent. Compare matching forms; added digestive ingredients remain separate.

guide.title: Betaine: TMG workout research and HCl digestive claims differ
guide.summary: Betaine anhydrous, also called trimethylglycine or TMG, is the main form studied for exercise. Betaine hydrochloride addresses a different product claim.
guide.evidence: A 2024 synthesis found a pooled strength benefit, especially in lower-body measures, with several other outcomes unchanged. A 2025 endurance review found sparse studies at high risk of bias. This is limited, outcome-specific evidence rather than a universal performance claim.
guide.limitations: Training status, study design and the tested outcomes vary. Anhydrous betaine findings do not establish digestive benefits for betaine HCl. A change in stomach pH from a small experiment does not prove relief of digestive symptoms or diagnose low stomach acid.
guide.catalogReading: Identify anhydrous betaine/TMG, betaine HCl or a blend. Keep explicitly labelled active and full compound amounts distinct; do not substitute equal grams of one form for the other or infer an anhydrous equivalent from compound weight. Check other pre-workout ingredients.
guide.safety: Digestive discomfort can occur. People using betaine for an inherited metabolic condition require specialist monitoring. Do not self-diagnose low stomach acid or change acid-suppressing medicines based on an HCl product claim; discuss symptoms and medicine interactions with a clinician.
guide.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Betaine is obtained from food and normal metabolism, then absorbed and used in several pathways.
It can donate methyl groups in the conversion of homocysteine to methionine and participates in regulation of cellular water balance.
Betaine HCl can lower gastric pH under specific experimental conditions. That acidifying property is a separate question from the exercise effects studied with anhydrous betaine.
guide.treatment: Specialist care can use betaine anhydrous as part of treatment for homocystinuria, a specific inherited disorder. That indication does not make a workout supplement a treatment for digestive problems or justify replacing a prescribed product.
guide.whoMayBenefit: An adult with a defined performance goal can review the modest and inconsistent exercise findings. A diagnosed metabolic condition needs a clinician-led plan; ordinary training or digestive symptoms alone do not establish a need for betaine.
guide.routineUse: No universal workout requirement for TMG or betaine HCl is established. Review formulation, reason for use and any amount already present in a pre-workout before considering another product.

whoCanConsider: Adult resistance-trained people with a specific strength objective can consider the limited findings for anhydrous betaine/TMG.
Adults comparing TMG with betaine HCl can first identify the form and intended purpose; exercise and digestive claims use different evidence.
whoShouldReview: People prescribed betaine for a metabolic disorder require specialist monitoring and should not substitute a workout product.
Persistent digestive symptoms or use of acid-suppressing medicines warrant clinical review rather than self-diagnosis of low stomach acid.
People with medical conditions, regular medicines, pregnancy, breastfeeding or under-18 use need individual guidance.
buyingGuide.foodSummary: Spinach, wheat products and beets provide naturally occurring betaine/TMG. Food betaine is not a betaine-hydrochloride digestive product or a prescription treatment.

value.targetedUse: A healthy adult resistance-training programme with a specific lower-body strength objective, evaluating anhydrous betaine/TMG as an optional adjunct.
value.reason: Some strength outcomes improve in pooled studies, while several others do not, and endurance evidence remains weak. This is situational value for a particular TMG context, not a broad performance or digestive recommendation.
worthWhen: The exact anhydrous betaine/TMG form and serving are disclosed and the intended outcome fits the evidence.
The buyer accepts modest, uncertain benefit and has checked whether a pre-workout already includes it.
skipWhen: Betaine HCl is being bought using TMG workout claims or nonspecific low-stomach-acid symptoms.
The expectation is a universal strength, endurance or fat-loss effect.
value.scope: The targeted rating concerns anhydrous betaine/TMG for a defined adult training outcome. It does not score betaine HCl, prescribe homocystinuria care or equate compound weights.

dos.title: Identify TMG versus betaine HCl
dos.detail: Check the exact chemical form and verified serving before comparing a product with the relevant evidence.

dos.title: Check existing formula overlap
dos.detail: Look for anhydrous betaine or TMG already present in your pre-workout before adding another product.

donts.title: Don't transfer claims between forms
donts.detail: TMG workout findings do not establish benefits for betaine HCl or equivalent active content from equal compound weights.

donts.title: Don't self-diagnose low stomach acid
donts.detail: An HCl product claim does not establish the cause of digestive symptoms or justify changing acid-suppressing medicines.

intakeGuide.summary: No established dietary reference intake or universal sports dose. TMG and betaine HCl have different uses.
notes: No automatic dose increase is assigned for training frequency or experience.

medicalGuide.summary: Condition-specific evidence, separate from sports benefits and purchase priority.

conditions.findings: Prescription betaine anhydrous is used with specialist care and other treatments. This indication does not apply to betaine HCl or establish equivalence of a workout product.
conditions.limits: Specialist care can use betaine anhydrous as part of treatment for homocystinuria, a specific inherited disorder. That indication does not make a workout supplement a treatment for digestive problems or justify replacing a prescribed product.

pathway.title: Betaine TMG and betaine HCl have different roles
pathway.summary: Anhydrous betaine, also called TMG, can donate a methyl group in homocysteine metabolism. Betaine hydrochloride is a different formulation studied for temporary stomach acidification.

steps.label: Cells receive available anhydrous betaine
steps.detail: Food, body metabolism and absorbed TMG contribute to the betaine supply.

steps.label: Betaine donates a methyl group
steps.detail: Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, present in liver and kidney cells, transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine.

steps.label: Homocysteine is converted into methionine
steps.detail: This reaction produces methionine and dimethylglycine. Its normal biochemical role does not establish an exercise benefit from extra TMG.

tracks.label: HCl formulation: a separate gastric effect

steps.label: Betaine hydrochloride reaches the stomach
steps.detail: This acid-containing formulation should not be treated as equivalent to the anhydrous TMG used in exercise research.

steps.label: The formulation increases gastric acidity
steps.detail: A small experiment gave betaine HCl after medication had suppressed stomach acid in healthy volunteers.

steps.label: Gastric pH falls temporarily
steps.detail: The trial measured a short-lived pH reduction, not lasting improvements in digestion, nutrient status or exercise performance.

pathway.caveat: Specialist betaine treatment for homocystinuria is a separate medical context. TMG workout claims and betaine HCl digestive claims require their own human outcome evidence.
